Metrical timing yields more anticipatory, less variable alignment with the unison model

Our third aim was to determine whether entrainment is a candidate mechanism for unison

production by investigating the temporal relationship between participant productions and the

unison stimuli in each prosodic timing condition. Overall, both groups of participants showed

evidence of temporal prediction in each timing condition, in that a substantive proportion of targets

“led” (i.e., were produced before) the stimulus (see Figure 2.7, productions represented to the

left of the vertical 0 crossing line). If participants were shadowing (i.e., listening, then speaking

reactively), we would expect their productions to consistently “lag” (i.e., be produced after) the

stimulus, reflecting the time required to perceive and then plan and produce the targets. Prior

research on shadowed speech, in which neurotypical participants spoke along with material they

had never heard before, has found that even the fastest shadowers still lagged the audio-recorded

stimuli at mean delays ranging between 250 and 300 ms (Marslen-Wilson, 1973). In the present

study, we found mean delays in this range only among three PWAs (Participants 902, 907, and

908), and only when they spoke along with conversationally timed sentences (see Table A.2) In

general, across conditions, mean timing offsets were below 200 ms for PWAs and were

consistently below 100 ms for controls. Compared to the study by Marslen-Wilson (1973), the

generally lower-latency (and in many cases, even anticipatory) timing offsets in the present study

are not entirely surprising, as participants in our study listened to each phrase twice before

repeating, enabling them to extract timing information that supports the subsequent planning and

production of speech in time with the unison model. Indeed, among neurotypical individuals,

similarly low timing offsets have been reported in studies of unison reading of familiar material, in

which the high degree of synchrony was attributed to entrainment, even though the material was

not metrically regular (Cummins, 2002, 2009). While methodological differences between these

prior studies and the present study may lead to slight differences in calculation of timing alignment

(e.g., accounting for line delay), the overall lower (and in many cases, anticipatory) timing offsets


<!-- Page 68 -->


50

in the present study support our hypothesis that entrainment underlies unison production of

familiar material. In other words, participants make use of timing information in the stimuli to

attempt synchronous spoken production in unison with the model. Evidence from finger tapping

studies may lend further support to this idea: It has been suggested that latencies less than 150

ms should be interpreted as evidence of temporal prediction, as this threshold may be the lowest

latency limit that reflects reactive motor response (Mates et al., 1992; Repp & Su, 2013). While

finger tapping is not entirely analogous to speech production, it is notable that many participants

in the present study exhibited mean timing offsets below this 150 ms threshold (see Table A.2),

which may further suggest temporal prediction rather than reaction. Finally, with regard to the few

PWAs who exhibited mean delays comparable to the shadowing delays in the Marslen-Wilson

study, it is worth noting that this only occurred in the conversational condition. In the remainder of

this section, we discuss the differences between conversational and metrical prosodic timing

conditions in the present stud, and interpretations relevant for findings among PWAs specifically.

Comparing prosodic timing conditions, we found that both PWAs and controls exhibited

less variable and more anticipatory timing alignment with the unison model when speaking along

with metrically timed stimuli compared to conversationally timed stimuli. This further supports our

hypothesis regarding entrainment, as it suggests that the increased rhythmic regularity of metrical

stimuli improves temporal predictability and facilitates subsequent production.  Previous research

has shown that when participants are required to tap along with a metronome, increased

variability is associated with poorer prediction and an increased tendency to lag the stimulus

(Repp, 2006). Our results show a similar pattern, evident when comparing the overall percentages

of participant productions that “led” versus “lagged” the corresponding targets in the unison model

in each condition, as well as differences in median SDoffset. As described above, in order for

participants to “lead” the stimulus—by producing spoken targets earlier in time than the unison

model—they must be able to anticipate the upcoming target. Comparing percentages across

prosodic timing conditions, metrical timing yielded a greater proportion of “leading” productions


<!-- Page 69 -->


51

for both PWAs and controls. With respect to variability, the lower median SDoffset  observed in both

groups indicates that metrically timed stimuli yielded enhanced stability in speech timing

compared to conversationally timed stimuli. In other words, participants were more consistent in

timing their spoken productions when the unison model had a more regular temporal structure.

We interpret the enhanced stability in this condition as evidence that metrical timing can

consistently facilitate the temporal aspects of speech planning and production during unison

production. This could potentially have clinical implications for determining types of treatment

stimuli that yield more consistent response during unison production, a possible avenue for

investigation in a future treatment study. Overall, it appears that the enhanced temporal prediction

afforded by metrical timing compared to conversational timing is evident not only in participants’

increased anticipation and resultant earlier production of upcoming targets but also in the reduced

variability of timing when speaking along with metrical stimuli.

It is important to note that despite this difference in proportion of leading versus lagging

productions in metrical versus conversational timing conditions, PWAs still lagged more than led

overall, including under metrical timing. However, this is not surprising, as while the rhythmic

regularity of metrical timing can provide a supportive temporal scaffold that both facilitates

prediction and lessens the demands on internally generating a timing framework for a spoken

production, it is unlikely to fully compensate for the disrupted language and motor planning

mechanisms characteristic of aphasia and AOS, respectively.

An alternate interpretation of these findings is that entrainment occurs only during

metrically timed conditions and that unanticipated factors related to our study design and

measurement yielded exceptionally fast shadowing among most participants in the conversational

condition, as well as some chance productions ahead of the stimulus targets. However, we find

this explanation unlikely, as participants heard all stimuli (including conversational stimuli) twice

before repeating in unison and were therefore afforded the same opportunity to extract timing

information based on these prior presentations, even if that timing information was more complex.


<!-- Page 70 -->


52

With the exception of a few participants with aphasia, the latencies found in the present study

were substantially lower than reported in prior shadowing studies (Marslen-Wilson, 1973), and

many were in fact similar to latencies described as evidence of prediction or entrainment in other

contexts (Cummins, 2002, 2009; Mates et al., 1992; Repp & Su, 2013). Furthermore, given that

PWAs by definition have difficulty with production of spoken output, it is likely that if they were

indeed shadowing in the conversational condition, they would exhibit latencies longer than those

reported for the “fastest” neurotypical shadowers, rather than latencies within the same range.

Thus, a more likely explanation is that our participants were not shadowing in either condition, but

rather using temporal prediction to guide an attempt at synchronous production of spoken output

when repeating in unison. Among most participants, this was reflected in a high degree of closely

aligned and even anticipatory timing. The rhythmic regularity of our metrical condition yielded

even less variable, more anticipatory timing, demonstrating better entrainment to the unison

model.

We remind the reader that, by our definition, metrical timing is not required for entrainment

to take place. Entrainment to conversational stimuli is possible (see Cummins, 2009) and even

potentially supported by the attentional bounce hypothesis (Pitt & Samuel, 1990), which proposes

that listeners allocate attention during speech tasks based on predictions about the occurrence

of upcoming stressed syllables but does not require that the syllables must occur in rhythmically

regular patterns. It is possible to make such predictions on the basis of other features, such as

syntax and information structure (see Beier & Ferreira, 2018), or—more likely for PWAs—other

external supports, such as written text as in ORLA (Cherney, 2010) and script training approaches

(e.g., Lee et al., 2009), or seeing the face and articulators of the unison model (Fridriksson et al.,

2012, 2015; Lee et al., 2009).

However, as is supported by work on temporal prediction and entrainment across domains

(e.g., Large & Jones, 1999; Pitt & Samuel, 1990; Thaut et al., 2015), we suggest that the rhythmic

regularity of metrical stimuli makes such prediction—and therefore entrainment—easier overall,


<!-- Page 71 -->


53

and can provide a useful scaffold for PWAs even in auditory-only unison production conditions

(Aichert et al., 2019; Kershenbaum et al., 2019; Racette et al., 2006).

Relationships between accuracy and entrainment at the individual level

As a final component of our exploratory Aim 4, we examined individual performance

patterns across all participants to determine whether individuals who speak more synchronously

with metrical unison models tend to exhibit better accuracy in this condition as well and whether

this gives rise to notable performance patterns across nonfluent and fluent subgroups of PWAs.

Nonfluent PWAs showed an apparent relationship between timing and accuracy: Of the

six nonfluent PWAs for whom we extracted timing data, five had significantly lower timing offsets

(indicating better prediction) when speaking along with metrical stimuli, and four of those five

produced a substantially greater percentage of accurate syllables in the metrical condition versus

the conversational condition (defined as score difference of ≥ 10 percentage points). This pattern

supports the idea that unison production broadly, and metrically based approaches more

specifically, are particularly well suited for nonfluent PWAs (Norton et al., 2009). We view this as

additional, more specific evidence that entrainment underlies the striking effectiveness of unison

production overall for this population and that metrical timing may confer an even stronger benefit

to accuracy.

Fluent PWAs did not show this relationship between accuracy and timing, as only two of

the eight participants had a significant timing advantage in the metrical condition, one of whom

achieved a substantially higher metrical accuracy score. There are a number of possible

explanations, though we recognize that they are somewhat speculative. First, as we have

suggested earlier, perhaps fluent PWAs do not need to rely as heavily on metrical structure as an

external scaffold to make predictions about upcoming targets and/or to generate timing

frameworks for their productions, as they are more able to rely on their relatively spared lexical

and syntactic processing resources to do so. Thus, their performance may in fact be similar across


<!-- Page 72 -->


54

both metrical and conversational timing conditions. If this is the case, we would expect a similar

pattern among control participants, who by definition have typical language abilities that they

could rely on during production. However, a considerable proportion of control participants (10

out of 18), exhibited significantly more anticipatory unison speech timing alignment in the metrical

condition than in the conversational condition. The difference in observable effect among fluent

PWAs versus controls might then be explained more specifically by differences in variance

between the two groups. Fluent PWAs may have underlyingly similar performance to controls—

generally comparable performance in metrical and conversational conditions, with a small benefit

from the metrical condition—but the effect may simply not be detectable in fluent PWAs due to

the increased variance in performance, which is characteristic of those with acquired brain injury

(Duncan et al., 2016). This would not be the case for nonfluent PWAs, who have poorer scores

in the conversational condition due to impaired language processing, and the substantial

difference in performance across metrical and conversational conditions “outsizes” the large

variance in performance in each condition, leading to a much larger observable effect. Due to the

small sample size of the present study, an attempt to investigate this idea empirically via subgroup

analyses would run a high risk of Type II error, but we hope to examine this possibility in future

work.

Another possible explanation for the lack of observable metrical benefit in fluent PWAs

may be that the metrical stimuli were distracting. There is evidence that metrical scaffolding may

not benefit everyone and may in fact have deleterious effects on performance for some: Hough

(2010) presented a case of an individual who had a successful response to MIT only when it was

modified to remove rhythmic hand tapping. His wife reported that he had found the tapping

distracting during prior treatment. Curtis et al. (2020) further suggest that some PWAs have

particular difficulty habituating to a beat, effectively rendering a rhythmically regular stimulus as a

constant reintroduction to a surprising element, which may compete with, rather than amplify,

online processing of other cognitive tasks. Our ongoing work includes assessment of musical beat


<!-- Page 73 -->


55

detection among PWAs, which will enable us to examine this possibility by investigating possible

associations between explicit rhythmic processing abilities and metrical benefit during

entrainment.

Lastly, it is also possible that the fluent versus nonfluent categorization of PWAs in our

study is too broad, obscuring potential patterns across participants that might be explained by

specific cognitive, linguistic, motor, and rhythmic abilities. Indeed, a primary goal of our future

work is to determine the specific clinical characteristics that may predict the effectiveness of

unison production and/or metrical timing for PWAs.

We have thus far focused on exploring the relationship between accuracy and timing in

PWAs in our study, but it is important to contextualize these findings by discussing this

relationship among controls as well. We found that the significant metrical timing benefit observed

for the majority (10 out of 18) of control participants was not associated with better syllable

accuracy at the individual level. However, this is not surprising; though controls as a group showed

a small but statistically significant metrical advantage for accuracy, no individual control exhibited

this pattern, and all controls achieved accuracy scores higher than 95%. As noted earlier, the

stimuli in this study were designed to capture variation in PWAs’ performance—not to tax a

typically functioning language system. Possible relationships among timing alignment, syllable

accuracy, and metrical structure among controls might be better revealed through a more

demanding task, such as nonword repetition or tongue twisters. However, the fact that many

controls were more time-aligned to the metrical stimuli than the conversational stimuli adds

evidence to existing research that has revealed a particular processing advantage conferred by

rhythmic regularity, measurable even among individuals with intact language abilities (Beier &

Ferreira, 2018; Pitt & Samuel, 1990; Quené & Port, 2005; Rothermich et al., 2012; Tilsen, 2011).

Conclusions

Overall, our preliminary findings support the idea that PWAs entrain during unison

production and that speaking along with metrically regular prosodic patterns facilitates temporal

prediction thereby supporting subsequent planning and production. This effect was most

pronounced in nonfluent PWAs in terms of both accuracy and timing of spoken output, which is

consistent with the longstanding clinical intuition that nonfluent PWAs are ideal candidates for

treatment approaches that employ unison production and/or metrical rhythm. However, benefits

associated with metrical stimuli were also observed for some fluent PWAs in this study, as well

as for control participants. These findings overall add to the evidence that rhythmic regularity may

generally aid spoken language processing across a variety of individuals—not just those with

restricted spoken output.

Limitations

There are some limitations of this study that are important to keep in mind. With regard to

our procedure, the present study employed a listen-then-repeat paradigm, which means that

participants became familiar with the stimuli before repeating them. In addition to facilitating

temporal predictability—the focus of this study—familiarity can also enhance lexical and semantic

prediction. To address this, we made an effort to match our metrical and conversational stimuli

such that prosodic timing structure was the only meaningful difference. However, we cannot

entirely rule out potential effects due to differences in lexical/semantic predictability between the

sentence stimuli for different timing conditions. In addition, the sample size is relatively small,

especially for subgroups of PWAs. Generalizability may also be limited by the lack of

representational diversity within our sample, which we plan to address in future recruitment

endeavors. In addition, while we broadly dichotomized PWAs here based on fluency, we

recognize that it does not adequately reflect the multidimensional nature of fluency (Gordon &

Clough, 2022), nor can it account for the substantial within-group heterogeneity in our sample.


<!-- Page 75 -->


57

While this heterogeneity enabled an interesting, preliminary exploration of interindividual

differences in performance, the present study did not specifically address the potential

relationships among specific cognitive, linguistic, and motor abilities that may be associated with

more success in metrical timing conditions. Some limitations in our statistical approach should

also be noted, particularly with regard to the timing alignment data for PWAs: We utilized Mann–

Whitney U-tests to maximize the amount of data from PWAs that we could meaningfully analyze

and to avoid underrepresenting participants with more severe aphasia in our analyses, especially

as these participants have typically been considered ideal candidates for metrical approaches

(e.g., Norton et al., 2009). However, this test formally requires independence of observations

rather than the paired observations (i.e., metrical vs. conversational timing offsets) that we

employed. Finally, this study did not examine whether the observed metrical benefit generalizes

beyond the immediate experimental context, potentially limiting overall clinical utility. In our future

work, we plan to expand the sample of participants with aphasia to improve statistical power to

the level required for more rigorous analysis techniques. We further aim to identify the key

behavioral variables that predict benefit from unison speech and metrical timing, with the ultimate

hope that this information can be used to optimize delivery of unison production treatments that

best match individual PWAs’ characteristics

## Introduction

The study described in Chapter 2 investigated the effect of prosodic timing structure on

(1) overall accuracy of sentences produced in unison with a spoken model, and (2) overall timing

alignment between the participant speech and the unison model. Group-level comparisons

revealed a greater percentage of accurate syllables produced under metrical timing compared to

conversational timing, and that metrically timed speech was produced both earlier (i.e., with

greater anticipation/less lag) between the participant’s output and the unison model), and with

less variability in time (lower standard deviations) relative to a unison model. We interpreted these

findings as evidence that the regularity of the metrical timing condition facilitated temporal

prediction, enabling better entrainment—a process described to support spoken production in

people with aphasia (Fridriksson et al., 2012; Quique et al., 2022).

The present chapter builds upon the previous study in several ways. The primary addition

is an investigation of the role of phrasal stress in our stimuli, to determine whether phrasally

stressed syllables differ from unstressed syllables in production accuracy and unison timing

alignment. The introduction that follows will describe the motivation for this exploration, including

the significance of phrasally stressed syllables as a feature of both conversationally timed and

metrically timed stimuli. A second addition is in the statistical approach. While the prior study

analyzed differences in central tendency across conditions, the present study implements

syllable-level regression models to directly examine which features of our experimental conditions

(unison vs. solo production) and stimuli (metrical vs. conversational timing, phrasally stressed vs.

unstressed syllables) predict production accuracy and facilitate temporal prediction. Finally, the

present chapter expands the data set, including additional people with aphasia (PWAs) and

control participants.

Defining phrasal stress

Chapter 2 introduced the contrast between metrically timed versus conversationally timed

sentences, arising from differences in the patterning of prominent, phrasally “stressed” syllables

versus non-prominent, “unstressed” syllables in each sentence type. While the patterns differ

across these two types of timing structures, both sentence types contain some syllables that are

stressed and some that are unstressed. There are important differences between stressed and

unstressed syllables—in terms of acoustic and linguistic properties, and in terms of how they are

perceived and produced—that make it logical to ask whether the beneficial effects of unison

production and/or metrical timing observed in Chapter 2 apply to all syllables, or specifically to

stressed syllables. Before discussing these differences and their implications in detail, we must

clearly define stress as it applies to the present study.

Stress has been described as “the linguistic manifestation of rhythmic structure” (Hayes,

1995, p. 1). It is a prosodic feature of many languages, characterized by the marking of a word or

syllable in a way that increases its salience relative to the surrounding context, sometimes termed

“phonetic enhancement” (Franich, 2022).  In spoken languages, stressed syllables are often

acoustically-phonetically enhanced compared to unstressed syllables, marked by longer duration,

greater intensity, and more extreme fundamental frequency  (Cole et al., 2019; Lehiste, 1970; see

also introduction to Franich, 2022).

In terms of English linguistic structure, there are two types of stress that are defined in

nested, hierarchical levels (Beckman & Edwards, 1994). Lexical stress refers to stress at the

single-word level, and can be most clearly illustrated in the context of multisyllabic words, where

one syllable is “stronger” than the others (e.g., baNAna, where capital letters indicate the stressed

syllable). Moving up the hierarchy, phrasal stress (also called sentence stress) refers to the

emphasis placed on one or more words within a phrase that signal(s) new and/or important

information to the listener. One way this can be illustrated is via sentences that contain the same


<!-- Page 79 -->


61

words, but contrast in the location of phrasal stress.1 In the sentence “She bought him a YEllow

banana”, the placement of phrasal stress (bold text) on the word “yellow” indicates the speaker’s

intent to clarify the color of the banana. In contrast, in the sentence, “She bought him a yellow

baNAna”, the speaker clarifies which type of yellow item was bought. Typically, the lexically

stressed syllable (shown in capital letters) within a phrasally stressed word is marked with a pitch

excursion, known as a pitch accent (Bolinger, 1958). Thus, a syllable can bear both lexical stress

as feature of the word structure, and phrasal stress as a feature of the phrase prosody. The

present study focuses on the role of phrasally stressed syllables, as they create the contrastive

patterns between our metrical and conversational sentence stimuli. However, the following

sections will review relevant literature pertaining to stress at both levels, as the rationale, design,

and findings of many of these studies overlap substantially and are therefore useful to consider

collectively.

Stressed syllables in spoken language perception and production

A number of studies involving individuals with typical speech/language abilities have

revealed processing advantages for phrasally stressed versus unstressed syllables, often by

investigating how rapidly and/or accurately participants detect specified targets embedded within

each type of syllable. For example, multiple studies have revealed that embedding targets within

stressed syllables leads to faster reaction times for target phonemes (Cutler, 1976; Cutler & Foss,

1977; Fiveash et al., 2021; Pitt & Samuel, 1990; Shields et al., 1974), and better accuracy in

detecting mispronunciations (R. A. Cole & Jakimik, 1980), vowel perturbations (Zheng &

Pierrehumbert, 2010), and word changes (Falk & Dalla Bella, 2016), and in recalling previously

heard target syllables (Gow & Gordon, 1993). In addition, tongue twister production experiments

1 Contrastive stress is used here to illustrate the concept, but readers should note that phrasal stress is a typical feature of spoken utterances, including those not serving to contrast alternatives. See Pierrehumbert & Hirschberg (2003) for additional information and examples.


<!-- Page 80 -->


62

have shown that phrasally stressed syllables are produced with fewer errors compared to

unstressed syllables (Croot et al., 2010; Kember et al., 2017).

A smaller set of studies has investigated relationships among syllable stress and spoken

language perception/production processes in people with acquired communication disorders.

Multiple experiments have shown that PWAs respond more accurately to comprehension

questions after listening to passages where target words were emphasized with phrasal stress,

compared to control conditions where there was no emphatic phrasal stress on target words

(Kimelman, 1999; Kimelman & McNeil, 1987). Similarly, emphatic phrasal stress has been shown

to improve reaction time and accuracy of semantic judgements in PWAs (Slansky & McNeil,

1997). With regard to production accuracy, most investigations have focused on the role of lexical

stress in people with aphasia and/or apraxia of speech (AOS), revealing that unstressed syllables

are more prone to errors, particularly in word-initial position (Aichert et al., 2016, 2019; Howard &

Smith, 2002; Nickels & Howard, 1999; though see Odell et al., 1991 for conflicting results). Similar

patterns have been revealed at the phrase level: Goodglass et al. (1967) found PWAs produced

phrase-initial unstressed functor words with more errors (or omitted them entirely), than when the

same words were produced with phrasal stress. One report of sentence repetition found that

people with AOS produced fewer errors on phrasally stressed content words (Tonkovich &

Marquardt, 1977). Finally, in one of the tongue twister studies described above, Kember et al.

(2017) found the same benefit of phrasal stress for people with dysarthria.

Overall, it appears that stressed syllables are advantaged in perception and production in

people with and without acquired communication disorders. However, as several studies with

PWAs note, relationships among stress and accuracy are complex and may depend on factors

related to linguistic structure as well as clinical characteristics of the participants (Goodglass et

al., 1967; Howard & Smith, 2002; see also Biran & Friedmann, 2005). As such, one aim of the

present study is to determine whether phrasally stressed syllables are produced more accurately

than unstressed syllables in our prosodically controlled sentence repetition task, which was


<!-- Page 81 -->


63

designed to systematically examine factors (unison production and metrical timing) that promote

accuracy of spoken output in people with aphasia.

Conditions that enhance temporal predictability

Why might stressed syllables be advantaged in perception and production? Some studies

have proposed that the increased salience of phrasally stressed syllables may aid listeners in

allocating attentional resources toward those syllables (Cutler, 1976; Pitt & Samuel, 1990; Shields

et al., 1974). Testing this attentional allocation idea, Cutler (1976) spliced acoustically identical

target words into sentences with differing intonational contours and found that participants were

faster at detecting phonemes within target words that were predicted to be stressed based on the

surrounding context. She interpreted this as evidence that predicting the location of upcoming

stressed syllables is “an integral part of sentence understanding” (p. 58). This idea later evolved

into the attentional bounce hypothesis, empirically tested by Pitt and Samuel (1990) through a

series of experiments using two-syllable words. In typical sentence contexts (akin to the

conversationally timed stimuli in Chapter 2), participants were more accurate, but not faster, at

detecting target phonemes in syllables predicted to be stressed versus unstressed (Experiment

1). In a follow up experiment, they used lists of two-syllable words, in which all words had stress

on either the first or second syllable, creating regularly alternating patterns of stressed and

unstressed syllables (akin in prosodic structure to our metrical stimuli). Here, they found that

participants were faster and more accurate at detecting phonemes in syllables predicted to be

stressed versus unstressed (Experiment 2), and that this finding did not generalize to word lists

with unpredictable lexical stress patterns (Experiment 3). They therefore suggest that anticipating

the location of stressed syllables does play a role in typical spoken language processing but is

enhanced substantially in contexts that are more rhythmically predictable.

Accordingly, an increasing body of research has examined how rhythmic regularity

(henceforth “metrical timing,” as in Chapter 2) may influence spoken language processing. Target


<!-- Page 82 -->


64

phonemes in stressed syllables were shown to be detected faster when syllables aligned with the

timing of strong beats predicted from the preceding metrical stimulus (Cason et al., 2015; Cason

& Schön, 2012; Quené & Port, 2005). In a more nuanced examination of metrical timing structure

and spoken language processing, Fiveash et al. (2021) conducted a syllable monitoring task using

metrically timed sentences in which participants were primed with metronome cues presented

either at the rate of phrasally stressed syllables, or at the rate of all syllables. Participants who

heard the phrasal stress prime earlier in the experiment were faster at detecting phrasally

stressed syllables versus unstressed syllables and were faster at this task than participants who

heard syllable-level primes first. There was no difference in reaction times to stressed versus

unstressed syllables for participants who heard syllable-level primes first. Thus, metrical stimuli

can establish top-down temporal expectations of phrasal stress structure and enhance processing

of phrasally stressed syllables. (See introduction to Chapter 2, as well as Beier & Ferreira, 2018

for additional examples of metrical timing and spoken language processing.) Building on this idea,

an additional aim of the present study is to determine whether the temporal predictability of

phrasally stressed syllables yields earlier timing during production when speaking along with a

unison model, and whether metrical timing enhances this effect.

Which aspects of temporal predictability benefit spoken output in PWAs?

Overall, the literature reviewed in the introduction so far suggests that (1) stressed

syllables (both at lexical and phrasal levels) are advantaged in speech/language processing and

production, possibly due to increased attentional resource allocation, and (2) metrical timing,

which enhances temporal predictability, can affect the processing of stressed syllables. From a

clinical perspective, these points are of particular interest in considering possible mechanisms of

unison production approaches for aphasia and AOS (reviewed more extensively in Chapter 2),

as stressed syllables are often the “locus of coordination” in speech synchronization behaviors

(Franich, 2022, p. 2, and references therein). Furthermore, a subset of unison treatment


<!-- Page 83 -->


65

approaches for aphasia use musical/beat-based prosodic timing, which typically involves

differentiating phrasally stressed syllables from unstressed syllables via higher pitch and/or

increased duration (Hurkmans et al., 2015; Norton et al., 2009; Van Eeckhout, 2010).  In addition,

multiple studies have revealed that metrical timing can increase overall accuracy of spoken

sentence production in PWAs/people with AOS  (e.g., Dworkin et al., 1988; Kershenbaum et al.,

2023; Racette et al., 2006; Stahl et al., 2011). However, the extent to which unison production

and/or metrical timing might differentially affect the production of stressed versus unstressed

syllables remains unclear.

Combining insights about phrasal stress, metrical timing, and unison production, a recent

study by Quique et al. (2022) found that PWAs were able to produce scripted sentences more

accurately following unison production treatment in which external rhythmic cues were added to

the model recordings, either aligned with the stressed syllables, or occurring with metrical

regularity throughout the sentence. Both types of rhythmic cues provided equivalent benefit to

overall production accuracy, but specific analysis of whether stressed versus unstressed syllables

were produced more accurately was not undertaken in that study. Thus, while a growing body of

work suggests that phrasal stress, unison production, and metrical timing can each benefit spoken

output in PWAs, it is unclear whether the increased temporal predictability of metrical contexts

and/or the scaffolding provided by unison production benefit the “beat-bearing” stressed syllables

specifically, or all syllables more generally.

As such, a third aim of the present work is to explore possible relationships among

accuracy, temporal predictability, and phrasal stress among PWAs. Understanding these

relationships can provide further insight into the mechanism by which unison production benefits

PWAs. We have previously proposed that unison production works by way of entrainment—a

process of predicting the timing of upcoming events in an external stimulus in order to produce

actions in time with that stimulus. The act of speaking in unison with a model requires the PWA

to generate temporal predictions about upcoming syllables, which may facilitate planning and


<!-- Page 84 -->


66

production of spoken output. Factors that enhance predictability may therefore further benefit

production. Results reported in Chapter 2 supported this idea, revealing through separate

analyses of temporal prediction and production accuracy that metrical timing benefits each during

unison production. Studies reviewed in this introduction suggest that stressed syllables are also

advantaged in temporal prediction (determined via perception studies) and production accuracy

(revealed in solo repetition). However, we have not directly explored the relationship between

temporal predictability and syllable production accuracy during unison production based on

metrical timing or stress status. If syllables that are better temporally predicted (produced earlier

in time) are also produced more accurately, this would provide more direct evidence for

entrainment as an underlying mechanism of unison production. Investigating stressed versus

unstressed syllables separately can shed more light on the nature of this mechanism: If the

advantaged status of phrasally stressed syllables is further enhanced during unison production

and/or metrical timing, this may suggest that the benefit associated with these facilitating contexts

is driven by amplifying resource allocation to those syllables specifically. However, it may be the

case that unison production and/or metrical timing aid prediction and production all syllables

equally. In either case, understanding how these variables relate to each other can provide

specific insight into how unison production works, which may have implications for designing

stimulus sentences that maximize treatment gains.

The present study

The present study is an exploratory investigation of the role of phrasal stress during PWAs’

sentence production under multiple speaking conditions, leveraging data collected for the study

reported in Chapter 2. In that study, we found that PWAs repeat sentences more accurately when

speaking in unison with a model (compared to repeating solo), and both PWAs and controls

produce unison sentences more accurately when sentences are metrically timed. In addition, we

found that metrical timing enhanced temporal prediction for both groups, as quantified by the


<!-- Page 85 -->


67

earlier and even anticipatory timing alignment of participant productions relative to the unison

model. Given the evidence that phrasally stressed (henceforth “stressed”) syllables may be

advantaged in perception and production, possibly due to enhanced temporal predictability (Beier

& Ferreira, 2018; Pitt & Samuel, 1990), and that the main contrast between our metrical and

conversational sentence stimuli is the patterning of stressed versus unstressed syllables, it is

important to understand how these variables may intersect. We investigate these ideas

systematically via the following exploratory Aims, and discuss potential hypotheses for each Aim

below.

Aim 1 focuses on production accuracy during sentence repetition, in which we ask whether

PWAs and/or controls repeat stressed syllables more accurately than unstressed syllables.

Additionally, we explore whether the effect differs based on production condition (unison vs. solo)

and/or prosodic timing condition (metrical vs. conversational sentence timing). We hypothesize

no effect of syllable stress among control participants. For PWAs, we hypothesize that overall,

stressed syllables will be produced more accurately than unstressed syllables across production

and timing conditions, and that the effect may be enhanced under metrical timing (and possibly

unison production), as the stressed syllables are made even more salient and predictable in the

context of a metrical structure. However, an alternative possibility is that metrical timing and/or

unison production improve production accuracy of all syllables, such that any beneficial effects of

phrasal stress are limited to the less predictable/scaffolded conditions of solo production and/or

conversational timing.

Aim 2 focuses on temporal predictability, as measured by comparing the timing alignment

between participant productions and stimuli in the unison condition. We ask whether PWAs and/or

controls produce stressed syllables with earlier timing alignment compared to unstressed

syllables, and whether the effect differs based whether sentences are metrically timed versus

conversationally timed. For both groups, we hypothesize that stressed syllables will be more

temporally predictable overall, such that timing alignment of stressed syllables will be earlier than


<!-- Page 86 -->


68

of unstressed syllables. We additionally hypothesize that this effect will be more pronounced for

metrically timed sentences, as we previously found that metrical timing leads to earlier-timed

productions overall (see Chapter 2). However, like our accuracy hypothesis, an alternative

possibility is that metrical timing enhances predictability of both stressed and unstressed syllables,

to the extent that any differential benefit of phrasal stress will be limited to conversationally timed

sentences, where temporal predictability is lower overall.

Finally, Aim 3 is the most exploratory, in which we examine relationships among accuracy,

timing alignment and phrasal stress to gain insight into the mechanism of unison production. We

hypothesize that syllables that are better temporally predicted (i.e., produced earlier in time

relative to the unison model) are more likely to be produced accurately, and further examine

whether this relationship differs for metrically timed versus conversationally timed sentences,

and/or for phrasally stressed versus unstressed syllables.

## Method

Participants

18 PWAs with post-stroke aphasia, 24 age-matched controls, and 24 younger controls

participated in this study. Controls had no history of neurological injury or communication

disorders. Table 3.1 contains demographic information for each PWA and summary information

for controls. Inclusion criteria were the same as the requirements outlined in Chapter 2. All

participants were required to pass a hearing screening with thresholds of ≤ 45 dB HL at 1, 2, and

repeat at least 50% of the words on the Single Word Repetition subtest of the BDAE-3, and score

within normal limits on two or more nonverbal subtests of the CLQT+ (Helm-Estabrooks, 2017).

Stimuli and Experimental Procedure

Stimuli and experimental procedure were identical to those described in the Method

section of Chapter 2. They are summarized here for clarity, but readers should refer to Chapter 2

for specific details. Briefly, stimuli consisted of 12 sentences with a metrical prosodic structure

and 12 with a conversational prosodic structure, audio recorded by a female speaker in a

soundproof booth. Metrically timed sentences contained repeating patterns of phrasally stressed

(S) versus unstressed (u) syllables (e.g., S-u-S-u, or S-u-u-S-u-u), while conversationally timed

sentences did not have repeating patterns. (See Figure 2.2A in Chapter 2 for a graphical

representation.) Sentences were developed in pairs to maximize lexical and phonological

similarity, while contrasting in prosodic timing structure (e.g.,“ASK me for EGGS at the MARket”

[metrical] vs. “reTURN the EGGS at the MARket” [conversational].) Metrically timed sentences

were recorded at a syllable rate of 2 Hz (120 beats per minute). Conversational sentences were

recorded using natural prosody and matched in duration to each metrical counterpart sentence.

Metrical were preceded by a lead-in sequence of metronome clicks generated based on the

metrical pattern of the sentence, while conversational sentences were always preceded by 4

metronome clicks.

During the experiment, participants listened to the sentences through over-the-ear

headphones, and then repeated them in two production conditions. During “solo” trials,

participants were instructed to listen to each sentence twice, and then repeat the sentence by

themselves. During “unison” trials, the sentence was presented three times: The participant

listened to the sentence twice, and then produced it in unison with the recording on the third

repetition. Thus, the 2 x 2 design (PRODUCTION CONDITION x TIMING CONDITION) yielded four

contrasts: Metrical Solo, Conversational Solo, Metrical Unison, and Conversational Unison.

Sentences were presented in pseudorandomized blocks by production condition to minimize the

cognitive load of alternating task demands. Audacity software (Audacity Team, 2021) was used


<!-- Page 91 -->


73

to present all stimulus sentences and record all participant productions. Unison trials were time

locked to the stimuli so that timing alignment between participant productions and the unison

stimuli could be evaluated. Line delay (presentation-to-recording delay) was documented at the

start of each experimental session for adjustment during analysis.

Stimulus rating: Determining phrasally stressed versus unstressed syllables

While stimuli were designed such that metrical sentences had obvious, regular patterns

of phrasal syllable stress and conversational sentences did not, the goals of the present study

required us to determine specifically which syllables in the conversational stimuli bear phrasal

stress. Past studies of phrasal stress perception in conversationally timed sentence contexts have

shown that listeners can vary substantially in which words they rate as “prominent” (Kakouros &

Räsänen, 2016; Mo et al., 2008; You, 2012). Therefore, rather than basing phrasal stress

assignment on the judgements of the first author, we opted for a systematic approach by

averaging ratings collected from multiple naïve listeners.

Five research assistants (RAs) with minimal to no familiarity with the stimuli in the present

study independently labeled the phrasal stress of the sentences after meeting with the first author

over videoconference for an orientation to the task. Each RA was provided a Microsoft Powerpoint

slide deck containing task instructions and two practice sentences, followed by a series of

individual slides for each of the 24 (12 metrical + 12 conversational) study stimuli. Though our

main motivation was to obtain phrasal stress ratings for syllables in conversational sentences,

metrical sentences were included for comparison to verify comprehension of the task. To avoid

potential order effects, sentence order was randomized in each presentation order, with the

exception that counterpart sentences (i.e., a corresponding pair of metrical and conversational

sentences) had to be separated by at least two intervening sentences.  Each stimulus slide had

one written sentence in the middle of the slide, and an audio icon in the lower left corner that

would play the corresponding sound file when clicked. To facilitate labeling, individual syllables


<!-- Page 92 -->


74

within multisyllabic words were separated by periods. Syllabification adhered to the Maximum

Onset Principle (Kahn, 1976) and was further verified with a syllabified version of CMU

Pronouncing Dictionary (1998; Bartlett et al., 2009). RAs were instructed to listen to each

sentence, and mark syllables that sounded “emphasized” or “prominent” in bold red text. Syllables

that RAs thought might be emphasized, or sound “partially emphasized” were to be marked with

italic text. RAs could listen to each sentence as many times as they wished, but were encouraged

to “go with their gut” perception regarding prominence.

RA ratings were converted to a trichotomous scoring system, with 0 for unmarked (non-

prominent) syllables, 0.5 for possibly or partially prominent syllables, and 1 for prominent

syllables. Ratings for each syllable were then averaged across all RAs, and any syllable with an

average score ≥ 0.75 was considered phrasally stressed in subsequent analyses. All others were

considered phrasally unstressed. Figure 3.1 shows the distribution of average rating scores in

each condition.

Average ratings for metrical stimuli were largely bimodal, and followed expected phrasal

Data scoring: Syllable production accuracy and interrater agreement

Participant productions were transcribed and scored by trained RAs, using a detailed

protocol similar to prior studies (e.g., Kershenbaum et al., 2019) and outlined in Chapter 2. Initial

syllables were discarded from analyses to account for onset difficulties. Remaining syllables were

then trichotomously classified and assigned numerical scores as follows: Correct syllables

received 1 point, syllables with one phonemic error received 0.5 points, and syllables with more

than one error (including complete omission) received 0 points. Each participant had a total of

388 scorable syllables (97 in each production condition x timing condition), apart from the

Data scoring: Unison timing alignment

The process for determining unison timing alignment between participant productions and

stimulus sentences was exactly as described in Chapter 2. In summary, we compared the voice


<!-- Page 95 -->


77

onset moment (VOM; the timing at which voicing begins) of obstruent-initial target syllables in

participant productions and stimuli. VOM was chosen as the point of comparison as (1) it is an

acoustic landmark that is relatively efficient to detect in the audio signal, and (2) it roughly

corresponds to the syllable’s “p-center,” a timepoint hypothesized as the location of the “beat” of

a syllable, and the point at which people have been shown to synchronize (Franich, 2022; Morton

et al., 1976). These VOM timepoints were used to calculate timing offset values for each target

syllable, defined as the signed difference in time between the participant’s VOM and the

corresponding VOM in the recorded stimulus sentence, subtracting line delay. Positive offsets

indicate that the participant’s production lagged the stimulus recording, while negative offsets

indicate that the participant spoke ahead of the stimulus, which we suggest is evidence of

temporal prediction. Importantly, target syllables were phonemically identical across each

metrical-conversational sentence pair to maximize comparability across prosodic timing

conditions (see Table A.1 for a complete list of stimuli).

VOMs were extracted from target syllables via a semi-automated procedure, using the

autoVOT plugin for Praat speech analysis software (Boersma & Weenink, 2021; Keshet et al.,

2014). We used Praat textgrids to manually isolate time windows around each target syllable

onset, which included the release burst of the initial obstruent consonant, four consecutive cycles

of voicing, and approximately 30 ms of padding on either side (see Chapter 2, Figure 2.3). These

time windows and associated audio files were input to the autoVOT plugin for Praat, which uses

a trained classifier to automatically detect and label multiple acoustic landmarks of voice onset

time within the specified time window (though the present study focused only on the VOM

landmark). During the window isolation process, any syllable productions that contained

phonemic errors, phonetic distortions, irregular pitch periods (“creaky voice”), or other possible

ambiguities were flagged for review. After running autoVOT, VOM timepoints were adjusted

manually as needed.


<!-- Page 96 -->


78

A maximum of 64 timing offset values (32 metrical + 32 conversational targets) were

computed for each participant, including for syllables produced with errors, as the present study

analyzes timing alignment separately from production accuracy. We made every effort to extract

VOM from all target syllables, however some participants had fewer than 64 total time points due

to (1) complete omission of the syllable, (2) no voicing of a vowel (e.g., “k—” for “con”), (3)

syllables for which the obstruent onset timing was too ambiguous to manually determine a search

window, and (4) audio recording error during data collection. Together, this resulted in

missing/excluded data for 11% of possible target syllables across PWAs (ranging from 1 to 19

missing targets per PWA), and for < 2% for possible targets across controls (ranging from 1 to 25

missing targets per control).

As a final preprocessing step, we excluded timing offset values that fell outside of +/- 2.5

SD of each individual participant’s mean time offset, separately for each timing condition. This

resulted in a reduction of less than 3% of timing offset data for PWAs, and less than 2% of control

data.

AOS construct score

To account for the extent to which AOS severity predicted syllable production accuracy

and unison timing alignment, an AOS construct score was calculated for each participant based

on performance on subtests of the ABA-2 (ee Table 3.3). Z-scores for each participant were

computed for Diadochokinetic Rate (DDK), Increasing Word Length Part A, Oral Apraxia, and

Repeated Trials (Raw) subtests, then averaged to obtain an overall AOS construct score. Higher

construct scores therefore reflect less severe AOS within our sample. A construct score based on

aphasia severity measures was not included as a covariate because it was highly correlated with

AOS severity in our sample. Furthermore, we deemed AOS more relevant to our questions about

timing alignment, as prosodic timing disruptions are considered to have diagnostic validity for

Statistical models

All statistical analyses were conducted in R, version 4.3.1 (R Core Team, 2023). Unless

otherwise noted below, all models were fit using the lme4 package, version 1.1-35.1 (Bates et al.,

2015), and p-values were computed using the lmerTest package, version 3.1-3 (Kuznetsova et

al., 2017). For logistic regression models, the lme4 optimizer was set to ‘bobyqa’ to avoid model


<!-- Page 99 -->


81

convergence difficulties. For significant interactions between predictors, pairwise comparisons

were investigated using the emmeans package, version 1.10.0 (Lenth, 2024). For readability,

model statistics for relevant results are reported in the Results section. However, full model

outputs for each analysis are included in the Appendix (Table A.3 through Table A.7).

To investigate the effects of phrasal stress, metrical timing, and unison production on

accuracy of syllable production (Aim 1), we fit separate mixed-effects logistic regression models

for controls and PWAs. These models included a crossed fixed-effects structure for experimental

predictors (PRODUCTION CONDITION * TIMING CONDITION * PHRASAL STRESS), and random intercepts

for participants. Reference categories for the predictors in this model were SOLO,

CONVERSATIONAL, and UNSTRESSED, respectively. AOS CONSTRUCT SCORE was included as a

covariate in the PWA model, and AGE (in years) was included as a covariate in the control model.

Age was not included as a covariate for PWAs as it was confounded by the heterogeneity of

clinical presentations across ages in our sample.

In both models, syllable accuracy was considered as a strict binary variable, where

syllables with any errors were considered incorrect. However, we note that such a strict approach

to accuracy could potentially obscure more nuanced relationships among production accuracy

and our experimental predictors, particularly for PWAs. Indeed, a notable percentage of syllable

productions among PWAs included syllables with only one phonemic error (e.g., “gog” for “dog”,

see Figure 3.6). Clinically, such productions can often be intelligible in context (Nicholas &

Brookshire, 1993), and could be considered a meaningful “intermediate” category of correctness

that might be separately predicted by one or more of our predictors. Thus, using the same fixed-

and random-effects model structure, we fit a mixed-effects multinomial logistic regression model

using the mclogit package, version 0.9.6 (Elff, 2024). In this model, the outcome contained three

categories of correctness: incorrect, one phonemic error, and correct. A multinomial model was

chosen rather than an ordinal model despite the ordered nature of the accuracy categories, as


<!-- Page 100 -->


82

our data did not meet the proportional odds assumption required for this model, determined

graphically using the procedure in Harrell (2015; p. 316).

To determine the effects of phrasal stress and metrical timing on unison timing alignment

(our measure of temporal predictability; Aim 2), we ran separate mixed-effects linear models for

controls and PWAs, with signed timing offset for each target syllable as the outcome. Signed

timing offset was used rather than absolute timing offset, as our hypotheses concerned prediction

(indicated by earlier-occurring productions) rather than absolute synchrony. The fixed- and

random-effects structure for each of these models was the same as for the accuracy models,

except that PRODUCTION CONDITION was not included since timing offset data existed only for

productions in the unison condition.

To explore possible relationships among accuracy, unison timing alignment, and phrasal

stress among PWAs (Aim 3), we visually inspected graphs of the timing offset data, stratified by

accuracy, across the levels TIMING CONDITION and PHRASAL STRESS. The relationship could not be

formally modeled with logistic regression, due to the difference in ranges of timing offset values

for the two prosodic timing conditions, which would lead to model overfitting and uninterpretable

odds ratios.

## Results
